title: The Only Thing the Houthis Have Done Successfully
excerpt: Yesterday in Riyadh, a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis struck King Khalid International Airport, killed 13 people, and wounded hundreds more
body: Yesterday in Riyadh, a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis struck King Khalid International Airport, killed 13 people, and wounded hundreds more
Attacks in the previous week had killed four others
Because Saudi Arabia has been trying for years to shed its reputation for austerity and discomfort, a sterile, boring airport with overpriced pastries and harsh lighting is a national accomplishment
The strike turned that airport into chaos, its floors streaked with blood and lounges billowing with smoke

The Houthi military spokesman announced that the attacks would continue on a reciprocal basis—“airport for airport, siege for siege, and escalation for escalation”—until the Houthis achieve their stated goals: the “death” of America, Israel, and their allies, and an apocalyptic victory for Islam
The Houthis hit the Riyadh airport again today

Saudi Arabia’s ongoing self-transformation during the past decade has involved trading cosmic goals—the spread of Sunni Islam over the world—for more modest local ones, such as opening specialty coffee shops in Jeddah and hosting pro-wrestling contests in Riyadh. (The two most prominent international events in the coming weeks in Saudi Arabia are an investment conference and World Wrestling Entertainment’s “Crown Jewel.”) One can imagine the frustration that Saudis feel, just as they try to exit the game of global religious domination, to be pulled back in by a neighbor far more zealous than they ever were
The Houthis “are on a divine mission,” Nadwa Al-Dawsari, an independent Yemeni researcher, told me last year

That mission, she said, is to “keep the war going, at least until Jerusalem.” Negotiation, for them, consists of tactical delay, so they can resume the fight and fight harder. “Why would they want a deal when they can get everything?” Earlier this week the Houthis’ leader, Abd al-Malik al-Houthi, delivered a typically long-winded denunciation of the Saudis
He devoted the bulk of it to condemning the Saudis for doing exactly what the Houthis have just done openly: targeting civilians
This decade-long conflict has indeed been characterized by a lengthy series of atrocities

Abd al-Malik listed alleged Saudi attacks against weddings, funerals, and homes—the total death toll far exceeding the missiles in Riyadh—and concluded that the Saudis were not Muslims at all but “Zionists” who follow “Satan.” He mentioned an attack on a market in Taiz, and said “there is absolutely no justification for targeting such a place,” because “it was a market, not a military camp.” Riyadh’s airport is also a civilian target, but I suppose because the Houthis think they are fighting Satan, they are willing to excuse their own hypocrisy. ( Here you can watch a group of travelers, dressed for pilgrimage to Mecca, blown off their feet.) What’s clear from the entire arc of the Houthis’ rise is that they are, as Al-Dawsari suggested, unwilling to negotiate, let alone go away or enter into what the Houthi leader describes as “an honourable peace with the Yemeni people,” “founded on good neighborly relations and mutual respect.” Sensible Saudi leaders would appease or join the Houthis, he said, but instead “they follow the Satanic approach.” Iran must be happy
Recently, Donald Trump has taken to gloating about the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, which now flows with oil traffic at near prewar rates

But the entire Iranian “Axis of Resistance”—the coordinate group including the Houthis, Iraqi Shiite militias, Hamas, and Hezbollah—was meant, as one American official put it to me, to be a keyboard on which many notes could be played, with rhythms able to keep the United States and its allies off the beat
Israel’s initial attacks against Iran in 2025 were an attempt to shoot the piano player
Iran has not only survived but also bragged that it has a surfeit of targets to select from

It is not a coincidence that just as Trump was congratulating himself for opening the strait last week, U.S. bombers had to scramble off the tarmac because of reported threats of an Iranian attack at RAF Fairford in England

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has a reputation for erratic decisions—sudden, apparently whim-driven plans to invest heavily in particular sectors, to pick fights with neighbors, or to oppress or kill this or that critic of his rule
He has been consistent, and indeed reasonable, in seeking, above all else, a path toward economic development uninterrupted by war or tumult
The main effect of this campaign by the Houthis is to disrupt that path
The Houthis are holding Saudi Arabia’s transition hostage by doing the only thing they have ever done successfully: fighting
It is not obvious that anyone has enough of a corresponding appetite for war to stop them.

title: Admiral McRaven: Public Execution Is Shameless and Ignoble
excerpt: A 62-grain, 5.56-mm round leaves the barrel of a standard-issue M4 rifle at approximately 2,900 feet per second
body: A 62-grain, 5.56-mm round leaves the barrel of a standard-issue M4 rifle at approximately 2,900 feet per second
When it strikes a human being, the results are violent, traumatic, and unpredictable
If Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has his way, such images will soon be broadcast to the American people
The Pentagon has announced that the execution of Nidal Hasan, the Army officer convicted of killing 13 fellow service members in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, in Texas, will be livestreamed
According to Amnesty International, 17 people were publicly executed in 2025
Eleven of these were in Iran and six in Afghanistan

Is this what we have become? Iran? Afghanistan? Are we so weak, so insecure, that we must convince the world that we are still powerful by making a public spectacle of an execution? Or maybe Secretary Hegseth and President Trump intend this as a spectacle for the American people: a show of just how much testosterone the two men have surging through their veins
But if Hegseth thinks that this public display will somehow deter others from horrible acts of violence, he is mistaken
Publicizing Hasan’s death therefore could incite other extremists to do equally egregious acts
And it adds to the narrative, advanced by our enemies and ever more worrying to our allies, that the United States has lost its way
When Osama bin Laden was killed, President Obama made a point of not releasing photographs of his body. “It’s not who we are,” he said
All of us who were involved in the operation agreed

Not sharing the pictures was a recognition that we are better than the inhuman beings who do unconscionable things, that there was a difference between a legitimate exercise of government authority and a public display of coercive power
Now, with this announcement, we are lowering ourselves to the ranks of brutal and failing regimes
I teach a graduate class on national-security decision making
I give my students a framework for thinking about how to make difficult decisions

The first question they have to answer before they can get to the right decision is: Who are we as a nation ? It is an acknowledgement that all correct decisions, those that will benefit us in the long run, will flow from an understanding of our American values

It’s not naive to think that we should have a sense of propriety when carrying out the harsh business of justice; to believe in our national sense of honor; and to expect our leaders to behave with dignity, integrity, civility, and humility
These values build stronger, smarter, more humane societies
They drive trust in businesses and higher education and they inspire our men and women in uniform
In almost 40 years of service, I came to realize that Americans share a common longing to be seen as the good guys
We were proud that our parents or grandparents fought against Nazism and fascism
As a nation, we stood tall against totalitarianism and communism
A younger generation sacrificed to keep America safe after 9/11
We made mistakes along the way; we always do
But despite these stumbles, inevitable in a complicated and violent world, I never once doubted that within our DNA was a sense of nobility that shaped the American character
There is nothing noble about a public display of a government-sanctioned execution
With this decision, the Trump administration continues to undermine our national values
Our current leaders are shameless and ignoble
They seem to believe that the performance of cruel power is what makes a nation great: the spectacle, the show, the crude theatrics of a tough guy
Just ask the oppressed people of Iran and Afghanistan.

title: A Spot-On SNL Parody About Men Who Can’t Deal With Time’s Passage
excerpt: Even if you don’t know much country music, you likely know how much the genre loves the trope of the weepy father at his daughter’s wedding
body: Even if you don’t know much country music, you likely know how much the genre loves the trope of the weepy father at his daughter’s wedding
In the best sketch of last night’s Saturday Night Live , the father of the bride was played by the host, Shane Gillis, but he wasn’t reflecting on life’s heavy milestones

Instead, he was thinking about “all the cool shit I can put in her room.” As narrated by a Rascal Flatts–esque band (composed of Andrew Dismukes, James Austin Johnson, and Tommy Brennan), the dad imagined everything he was going to put in his new man cave: a Ms

Pac-Man machine and a pinball machine; a drum set that he swore he would finally learn to play; a life-size cutout of Shaquille O’Neal; a bottle of lotion and box of tissues (a bit stolen from the Paul Rudd film I Love You, Man); a House box set; a cotton-candy machine
A child’s wedding is a joyous occasion, a new chapter for the family
But any beginning also reminds us that time’s arrow stubbornly points in only one direction
The sketch smartly underscored how many American men use consumer goods to distract themselves from anxieties about aging and the creeping sense that life may pass them by

Why deal with your uneasy feelings when you can finally afford the replica of a Star Wars stormtrooper you’ve wanted—nay, deserved—since you were a teenager? The hit of dopamine from a shopping spree is certainly more fun than wrestling with where your life currently stands
The best SNL song sketches expand on a central idea as the parody progresses, commenting on the characters’ comedic dilemmas

They also need to nail the musical references (Tim McGraw, Alan Jackson, Zac Brown, and, yes, Rascal Flatts have all released songs on this theme, something that the southerners Dismukes and Johnson are likely aware of)

In last night’s sketch, we learned that Gillis’s presumably long-suffering wife (Ashley Padilla) “hates my room / we’re drifting apart,” and that she’s becoming a bit too close with her Zumba instructor, Tad (Marcello Hernández), “who’s actually pretty cool”—an off-hand remark from a man too clueless to see what’s coming next

Whatever you think about him, last night’s host was well equipped for this exploration of male obliviousness. [ Read: What Shane Gillis proved on SNL ] In 2019, Gillis was set to join SNL before some of his old offensive jokes resurfaced and NBC rescinded the offer
Gillis apologized for the material, and SNL ’s creator, Lorne Michaels, indicated that the casting decision was out of his hands
Michaels seems to have some lingering regrets about how it all went down; last night was Gillis’s third time hosting
But this overcorrection is arguably not doing Gillis many favors, as the episode often demonstrated his limitations as a comedian
He flubbed most of his lines—and cursed—in a sketch parodying Green Eggs and Ham , then apologized “about earlier” during the episode’s closing goodbyes
Gillis tends to embody characters who aren’t actively hateful or toxic but just a little confused about society’s changing social mores and unsure about what they’re allowed to say
But Gillis, who lacks the dexterity of clear influences such as Louis C.K. and Dave Chappelle, can’t consistently pull off that tricky balance of thoughtfulness and provocation

During his opening monologue, in a bit about struggling to seem nonthreatening when he encounters a woman on an otherwise solitary hike, he lost the audience after saying, “I haven’t been to the gym in so long I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” (I’ll spare you his description of women’s modern athleisure wear.) By that point, the crowd was so cold he couldn’t win it back with a clever closing riff about society’s polarization and the dangers of ambiguous haircuts: “You’re either gay or you’re Hitler, and isn’t that where we’re at as a country?” Still, Gillis has become a successful touring comedian, mostly because he is very good at expressing the immaturity, simmering hostility, and general dunderheadedness of a certain strain of American manhood

His best sketches from last night made use of that meathead persona, as when he played a jerky police officer hosting the discussion show Cop Talk and the manager of an HVAC company that prided itself on having the most off-putting employees you would ever encounter
But the wedding-song sketch stood out because it zeroed in on the stunted emotional life of Gillis’s character and then mocked it relentlessly

After his wife left him for Tad, he decided to build an even bigger room of one’s own (“Super Room Rocks!”), but when the impromptu construction project exposed him to black mold, he began “tripping balls.” The story eventually took an unexpectedly frisky turn before the episode’s kicker revealed this entire misadventure was a dream sequence that began after he forgot to help his daughter and wife pack up the moving van—a sly commentary on the character’s misplaced priorities

It’s hard to say whether Gillis found success because he’s secretly very perceptive about the state of modern masculinity or because he’s unafraid to admit just how unperceptive he is about the modern world

Either way, last night’s song fulfilled the country-music imperative of “three chords and the truth”: a catchy ballad about how many men are emotionally stunted and unable to deal with aging and change, and will instead retreat into materialism and adolescent interests rather than reconcile with life’s relentless momentum.

title: I Thought I Was Good at Something
excerpt: and then I lose an hour to those billiard-trick-shot videos, magnificent, their impossible spins, flawless timing, the punctuated clunk of the corner pockets li
body: and then I lose an hour to those billiard-trick-shot videos, magnificent, their impossible spins, flawless timing, the punctuated clunk of the corner pockets like God exhaling just a little
There’s the one where the cue ball kisses every single solid in procession as if in a receiving line before sinking the eight
There’s the simple shot, a spin so hard, the cue circles back on itself only a few inches away to sink a ball exactly behind it
If I have a name I will need you to remind me
But then it’s today and something snaps in me like a glowstick, bright and temporary
My mother phones and starts talking about identifying possum tracks in the snow
Isn’t it summer? I think and venture out in the city

I get on the train, head to whatever job I recall having had but still the world is here too much and like an eclipse it’s bad for you to look at directly, the naked tenderness of the men reading self-help books on the train—all their failures and desires written right there on the covers
I surface to the streets of this city made crazy with commuters, how perfect we are, moving toward what it is we chase
How one by one we drop into the manholes on the corners with a clunk.

title: Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI
excerpt: B ecause literary journals tend to have small circulations, few readers are likely to have come across “ The Whistleblower ,” a short story by the Zimbabwean wr
body: B ecause literary journals tend to have small circulations, few readers are likely to have come across “ The Whistleblower ,” a short story by the Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza
Published in 2021 in a journal called Transition , the story is a taut and closely observed political thriller in miniature
Its narrator, a sharp but inexperienced computer-science graduate in Harare, Zimbabwe, encounters an intelligence officer at the mall—a former teacher of his—who now wants something from him

At first, the graduate is nervous for what turns out to be the wrong reason: “I’d had a brief relationship with his niece Agatha and I wasn’t sure whether he knew about this or how he felt about it if he did.” A more recent story with Kundizeza’s name on it, “ The Blue Fighter ,” will surely find its way to more readers
Last week, it was named the winner of the prestigious Caine Prize for African Writing, which awards 10,000 British pounds (about $13,000) for a short story by an African writer
Some previous winners, including Namwali Serpell and NoViolet Bulawayo , are now among the world’s most celebrated authors
Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad—maudlin and full of tired tropes

Here, the Zimbabwean narrator is the son of a hapless father who squanders the family’s money trying to breed fish in tanks, to the mother’s chagrin. “‘We can’t afford this house anymore,’ she said one evening, placing the notice in front of him while he tested the seal on his newest creation,” the story reads. “Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come.” At the end, the narrator compares the last remaining fish to his family: “Not broken, just learning how to live differently
Still here.” That this narrator has all the personality of a chatbot is probably not coincidental

The AI detector Pangram flags almost the entire story as AI-generated; a notable exception is its epigraph, also about a father with a fish fixation, which is excerpted from what’s described as an unpublished poem by Vangile Gantsho
This isn’t the first prize-winning story to be flagged by Pangram
It comes after similar scandals over this year’s Commonwealth Prize and Prix Goncourt —two other renowned literature contests—in which Pangram flagged AI use among finalists

In the case of the Commonwealth Prize, one of them eventually won ; the Prix Goncourt pulled a writer from consideration after suspected AI use was compounded by plagiarism allegations over his earlier work
Any of these incidents might have been written off as a fluke

Together, they point to something of a crisis of trust—in both writers and technology—that threatens to undermine a global system of literary recognition. [ Read: The literary AI scandal that changes everything ] AI detection is fallible , which has raised concerns among some readers and writers about the prospect of false positives

But Pangram, which uses AI for its classification of text, is highly accurate : The company says its tool mistakenly labels human text as AI in about one in 24,000 cases; outside research also finds false positives to be extremely rare

When I ran all 25 of the previous Caine Prize-winning stories through Pangram, it labeled them as 100 percent human-written; the same is true of Kundizeza’s “The Whistleblower.” I reached out to Kundizeza about Pangram’s assessment of “The Blue Fighter” through his agent, Adrienne Ingrum at the Serendipity Literary Agency

She wrote that Regina Brooks, the agency’s CEO, would send me “evidence that the author and we at Serendipity are completely confident that the story is Simba’s own work.” Neither Ingrum nor Brooks followed up before publication
I also spoke at length with Ellah Wakatama, who chairs the Caine Prize’s board of trustees
Wakatama, a longtime book editor, told me that AI-generated fiction is not eligible for the prize
As soon as she learned of an inquiry I’d sent about the Pangram assessment of Kundizeza’s story, she and her colleagues initiated an investigation and contacted the author
Wakatama told me that she and a colleague will interview the prize judges, and that she’ll reread Kundizeza’s story and talk with him in detail about his methods
She added that a colleague has been in contact with Kundizeza’s agent about whether a verification process might include, say, reviewing previous drafts

Yet Wakatama forcefully rejected the notion that an AI detector could, or should, be used to gauge AI involvement. “My stance, as the person who leads the prize, is that if there is such an accusation, I want proof that does not come from a machine.” She said she planned to approach Kundizeza with “compassion” and the presumption of honesty

Wakatama is also Zimbabwean. “As an African,” she said, “my first stance is, if I ask you, Are you telling the truth? and if you say yes, I am going to believe you—especially because the accusers are not coming from amongst our own people.” Wakatama remarked on details in Kundizeza’s story that strike her as so typically Zimbabwean that a Zimbabwean must have written them: the shame of moving from a nice suburb to a less privileged township; how the mother’s initial forbearance with the father gives way to taking matters into her own hands
Wakatama also perceives multiple layers of meaning

She doesn’t think AI models are capable of that kind of cultural or literary nuance. [ Read: The Pangram backlash unfolding on college campuses ] But then, she acknowledged that she doesn’t use AI or AI detectors. “My first response when somebody asks me to use AI is that I think about water and energy,” she said—that is, AI companies’ excessive use of both. “That honestly overwhelms me, and I don’t want to.” Wakatama isn’t involved in choosing the Caine Prize winner—a panel of judges reads all the submissions—but her approach to AI is common among organizations that award prizes or other honors to writers

Partly, this is a pragmatic response to the risk of false positives. “Our legal parameters don’t allow us to contest the honesty of our writers just because a tool says that,” Razmi Farook, the director-general of the Commonwealth Foundation, told me during the scandal over its prize
But this wariness also reflects a general aversion, in literary and arts circles, to engaging with AI products, even if just to understand them better—including Pangram
The start-up’s product itself is based on AI, and it belongs to the Silicon Valley ecosystem; the company recently raised $50 million in funding, according to a person familiar with the deal
The skepticism is easy to understand, but it might be shortsighted
Research suggests that the people most familiar with AI output excel at sniffing it out
I’ve covered AI for almost a decade, and have written fiction for even longer; in short, I’ve had plenty of exposure to both literature and chatbot output
I know from experience that, for example, AI models aren’t terrible at picking up on cultural details

When I read “The Blue Fighter,” I was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions ; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms. “Anger burns out eventually,” the narrator’s mother says at one point. “Hunger doesn’t.” The earlier story by Kundizeza lacked those stylistic qualities, its prose and dialogue far more plainspoken and natural-sounding: “So how are things with my niece, huh?” the intelligence officer asks at one point

What I also noticed, more disturbingly, was the presence of stereotypes about African life common among outsiders: a blundering, unemployed father; a resilient matriarch who dispenses clichéd approximations of wisdom; an environment of deprivation

Research consistently shows that AI products reproduce cultural tropes , including those having to do with the African continent . [ Read: The most famous AI writing tic is also the most mysterious ] The novelist and critic Tope Folarin , a former Caine Prize winner who has written about how dominant white culture shapes global literature, told me after reading the story that it would be unfortunate if Kundizeza had relied on AI for any of it, because its plot is “deeply human” and “deserves human expression.” He also said, “There are a lot of writers from the global South who feel this extreme pressure to write to expectations so their work is legible to the West, and obviously chatbots have glommed onto that.” He called the incident a “tragedy.” Wakatama, for her part, explained her suspicion of AI detection by referencing the long , fraught history of science being used to oppress people of color
To a skeptical reader, her invocation of race might sound like a preemptive excuse
But in our conversation, she came across as open-minded and intellectually honest
I considered her wariness of Silicon Valley well founded and reasonable—particularly because the writers implicated in three major literary scandals this year were all nonwhite and non-American

title: Do Human Beings Have Souls?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The majority of Americans believe that every human being has an immaterial soul, and they tend to base their
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube The majority of Americans believe that every human being has an immaterial soul, and they tend to base their sense of human dignity and equality on this belief
Yet the culture at large often operates under the assumption that physical reality is all there is

Which view is correct? In this episode of The Permanent Questions , self-described “spookiest” David Brooks talks with Shelly Kagan, a best-selling philosopher who insists souls do not exist—and that we don’t need them in order to embrace the wonder and mystery of human experience

The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: I think the essayist Meghan O’Gieblyn was accurately capturing parts of America when, in her book God, Human, Animal, Machine , she wrote, “It is meaningless to speak of the soul in the 21st century

It has become a dead metaphor, one of those words that survive in language long after a culture has lost faith in the concept." Yet here’s the funny thing: According to the Pew Research Center, 85 percent of Americans say that they have a soul
They really do believe they have a mystical, immaterial, spooky, ghostlike thing at the center of who they are
And I have a confession to make: I’m one of those people
Furthermore, this metaphorical and spiritual meaning of the word soul is pretty central to the way I see the world
Long before I ever believed in God, I was firmly convinced that each person you meet has some piece of themselves that has no size, weight, color, or shape, but gives them infinite value and dignity
In today’s conversation, we’re gonna address the question: Do humans have souls? I’ve laid my cards on the table
We’re gonna be joined by Shelly Kagan, and he does not think we do
Kagan is the Clark Professor of Philosophy at Yale University
For over 40 years, stretching back to his days at the University of Illinois, Chicago, he has taught a course on death to undergrads, which, naturally enough, takes up the subject of the soul
Shelly Kagan (from lecture): Last time, I distinguished between two ways in which thinking about the facts about the nature of death could influence our behavior
On the one hand, it could give us reasons to behave or respond differently, and on the other hand, it could merely cause us to behave differently
The course has become globally famous because it’s on YouTube
Those lectures have been seen 33 million times in China alone
Part of his success is his intellect, but part derives from the fact that for a guy who doesn’t believe in enchantment, he’s a completely enchanting guy
I’m pleased to welcome Shelly Kagan to this table
Shelly Kagan, welcome to The Permanent Questions
Now, there’s a chapter in your life I’m confused about
It concerns the time you go to Wesleyan in 1972
You grew up in Skokie, Illinois, right? Shelly Kagan: That’s correct
Brooks: And you go to Wesleyan, and you’re a religion major for some period of that time
But you also read John Stuart Mill’s Utilitarianism , which suggests to me that you’re trending in the direction you’re trending, which we’ll talk about
But then in your senior year, you apply to rabbinic school
So in my mind, you’re trending toward a utilitarian, maybe non-believing form of life, and then you apply to become a rabbi
What’s up with that? Kagan: I had planned to be a rabbi starting at some point in high school, and that was what I anticipated all through college
As you say, I applied to rabbinical school, a particular rabbinical school, in fall of my senior year
I got the rejection letter, spring of my senior year

So I graduated from college and was suddenly in the situation that most of my friends had been in for four years, asking myself, So what do I want to do with my life? I thought I had known what I wanted to do with my life
But I had already come into college knowing I was also interested in philosophy, which, as it happens, I’d gotten into through Judaica

Brooks: I guess my question is: Did you believe in God, and you thought, Well, I’d like to serve God by being a rabbi ? Kagan: Well, I believed in the importance of Judaism, and I suppose any traditional Jew will say something like, “I believe in God.” But what it is to believe in God—as I imagine you know—from the Jewish point of view, that’s left much more up to you
Judaism doesn’t have a central set of religious dogmas
How you interpret this, as well as other central Jewish thoughts, like revelation—there are rival thinkers
Judaism was important to me through college
Judaism stayed important to me after I got rejected from rabbinical school

After college, I asked myself, Should I reapply to rabbinical school? Should I get a secular Judaic degree? Or—and this was literally the very first time the question ever crossed my mind— Maybe I should become a philosopher
Since I thought I had known what I was going to do, the question had literally never occurred to me

Brooks: When you thought about philosophy, did you think, I just wanna talk about big ideas , or is it, Like being a rabbi, I’m sort of ministering to people’s minds ? Kagan: I think it’s not a coincidence that of all the different topics in philosophy, the area I ended up specializing in is ethics and moral philosophy

title: Your kid wants to go vegan. Should you let them?
excerpt: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
body: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave
I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond
Please send in any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have
Neither of her parents are even vegetarian — we’re “free range chicken/grass fed beef” types
She has learned about veganism from friends at school, and seems to have come to her position more or less on her own
I want to encourage her ethical choices, but her mother and I agree that children should be introduced to new foods and flavors at this age
She has no allergies or intolerances that we know of
I worry that making accommodations for her dietary restriction may lead to a lifetime of picky eating, even if hers is a reasonable and ethical approach
She seems to be uncomfortable when her mother or I cook meat for meals we share, even if we make her another option
What should I do to support my daughter? Dear Hold the Beef,  When I was around your daughter’s age, I went to Hawaii with my parents
One night, we ate dinner on the beach, and we watched as a pig was dug up from an underground steam oven
I was horrified to see its face and nose; most of the meat I had eaten so far in my life didn’t resemble the animal it came from

A few years later, I became a vegetarian, and then in my 20s, a vegan.  Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! I share this story to reveal my slight bias in answering your question, but also my understanding of the ethical awakening your daughter might be experiencing
As you figure out how to talk to your child about what she decides to eat, we can at least table discussing the pros and cons of veganism itself

Instead, you should think about what amount of autonomy your child should have, and whether the moral decision-making she wants to engage in matches with her current stage of development.  People don’t turn 18 and then suddenly start engaging morally with the world
As we grow up, we try to understand right and wrong in fits and spurts

Lawrence Kohlberg, a 20th-century American psychologist, is best known for attempting to track a person’s moral development throughout their life.  Kohlberg presented people with hypothetical dilemmas in order to come up with six moral stages
In one example, he asked people of different ages about a dying woman who could be cured by a drug that was cheap to make, but that a manufacturer was charging an exorbitant fee for
The woman’s husband ends up stealing the drug

Is that right or wrong? Kohlberg observed that in answering questions like this, young children have what he called a “preconventional morality”: Their notions of right and wrong are dictated by what their parents think, and the avoidance of punishment when breaking those rules

For instance, the main reason not to throw your dinner on the ground or hit your brother was to avoid consequences from parents, not a feeling that there’s something wrong about that action.  Kohlberg thought this stage lasted until around age 9, and in the next period, children began to understand that there isn’t just one correct action, but that people could have different moral ideas based on their social context

To sum up the rest of the stages quickly, each one progresses to encompass more views — like the moral agreements necessary to make a society function — and more complexity — like the realization that a seemingly immoral action can ultimately be moral, like stealing medicine for one’s wife.  It’s useful to pinpoint where your daughter finds herself on Kohlberg’s timeline
It sounds like she’s in the shift from the first stage and into the later ones
What you’ve decided — that it’s okay to eat meat if it’s free-range or grass-fed — is no longer sufficient for your daughter in terms of guiding her own actions
That can be a jarring moment for a parent, but at least, according to Kohlberg, it’s a sign of maturation
Your child should , at this age, start to consider her friends, as well as the experiences she’s had without you, when making an ethical choice.  But I’m her parent , you may protest

That doesn’t necessarily mean that your job is to exclusively provide black-and-white directives.  Alison Gopnik, a psychologist and philosopher at the University of California Berkeley, has written about the unique perspective and personhood of children (including babies)
In her book The Gardener and the Carpenter , she questions how people have come to define the act of parenting as having specific goals in mind for their children
This approach is like being a carpenter, she writes, who follows instructions to assemble a predetermined piece of furniture
She argues that parenting is more like gardening: You cultivate the soil and the environment and realize that you could produce any number of different flowers, fruits, or vegetables

Growth is the point, not a by-the-book final product.  I see Gopnik in alignment with Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the 18th-century philosopher whose novel Émile, or On Education surprised its readers by advocating for a freer and child-centered approach to teaching. Émile, a young wealthy boy, is tutored — in high contrast to the expectations of the day — without strict rules
Rousseau thought you couldn’t make a child turn into an adult any faster, and it was foolish to try

He also thought that children had to learn by having their own experiences out in the world, and learning from those, rather than just overly didactic lessons.  As your daughter dips her toe into the morality of eating meat, Rousseau would also remind you not to expect her to have the most mature ideas about veganism or her meal plan
She is still young, and may just have come across an idea that feels ethically important to her
Your role as her parent is to help her develop her nuanced morality, a process Kohlberg suggests will continue, and not steer her towards one way of eating over another
Be Gopnik’s dietary gardener, not carpenter.  Of course, parents do have rights over their children, and an obligation to keep them safe
When we’re young, we’re not always equipped to make the right choice (some would argue this continues into adulthood, too)
If your daughter decided to take up smoking cigarettes, for instance, you would step in because her choice would negatively affect her health

title: The company behind Skittles might be to blame for your big vet bills
excerpt: Nova, a 6-month-old Australian shepherd, gets vaccinated at the Community Animal Medicine Project, a low-cost veterinary clinic in Northridge, Los Angeles, on J
body: Nova, a 6-month-old Australian shepherd, gets vaccinated at the Community Animal Medicine Project, a low-cost veterinary clinic in Northridge, Los Angeles, on July 7, 2026. | Hans Gutknecht/MediaNews Group/The Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images Whenever I have dinner with friends, the conversation always ends up on one of three topics: how hard dating is , the hunt for affordable housing , or an update on everyone’s pets
The last on that list includes cute photos and veterinarian updates
I love hearing about my friends’ cats and dogs
But I also have to admit that I just don’t get it
I never have. (We won’t discuss the ill-fated caterpillar in elementary school.) I’m in the minority: Over half of American households have pets
Which means that over half of American households have also seen the cost of pet care go up in recent years.   Helaine Olen is the proud pet parent of a Havanese poodle mix named Barney Rubble

She’s also the managing editor at the American Economic Liberties Project, an antitrust organization, and she says people often aren’t prepared for how expensive it can get.  Some of it is inflation, Olen says, but veterinary care is a major factor. “The same medical advances that have kept us alive longer and we consider miracles — whether it’s cancer drugs or stem cell therapies or various pharmaceuticals — the same is true for your cats and dogs,” Olen says
Decades ago, a cat having an MRI was unheard of; now, it’s common
But it’s not just expanded access and improved technology that’s driving prices up

Olen says that who’s behind that healthcare is a factor. “Big corporations and private equity have seen all of this, know that people say they will do anything for their pets, know that they think of their pets as children, and they have rushed into the sector,” she told Vox

So how did private equity get involved in the lives of our pets? And what happens when the prices keep climbing? We discuss that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me , Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.  Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Olen, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545
What kind of costs are we talking about? When your pet is young, you’re probably spending several hundred dollars a year for various vaccines, spay and neuter, annual checkups
But the real costs start coming in as they get older and they need maintenance.  For tooth cleaning, pets need to be put under anesthesia
That will be even higher if a pet’s tooth has to be removed.  I’ve spoken to people whose pets have back legs that have collapsed or disc herniations
You can easily be out over $10,000 on a surgery
You can easily spend four figures on a 24-hour overnight
I spoke to somebody who was quoted $3,500 a night for just an observational overnight
You mentioned that some of this comes down to who owns pet clinics and how that’s changing
Who owns them now? Traditionally, it was an independent practice
But in the past 10 to 15 years, big corporations and private equity have moved into the space
The largest owner of vets in the United States right now is a group called Mars
And if Mars sounds familiar to you, that’s Mars as in Skittles.  They own around 2,500 vets under the names of VCA, Banfield, and Blue Pearl
I’d say somewhere between a third and 50 percent of vet clinics are owned by corporations
It was 10 percent or less than 10 percent a little over a decade ago

What caused this spike and why is a candy company behind it? As people realize how much can be done to help their pets, the corporations and private equity basically saw what one analyst described as low risk, high reward

I’ve spoken to employees of some of the larger chains who have told me that prices went up routinely every six months or every nine months or once a year.  In Britain, there was a recent government investigation into all of this by the Competition and Markets Authority, their equivalent of the Federal Trade Commission

They determined that private equity and corporate ownership is responsible for a billion pounds spent on pets over a five-year period that otherwise wouldn’t have been spent, and that people were paying about 16 percent more at vets owned by large corporate outfits versus independent vets

How are people paying for this if it’s so expensive? I live in Los Angeles, and I wrote a piece for New York magazine a few months ago about all the people here who are now driving their pets down to Tijuana because it is so much less expensive down there.  Pet insurance is a very mixed bag
My own pet insurance increased by 30 percent from last year to this year
And by the way, my dog Barney Rubble is 2 and a half years old

He has had no issues that I am aware of that would account for a 30 percent increase.  The other thing with pet insurance, unlike human health insurance, is there is no preexisting [conditions] clause
I have lost count of the number of people I’ve interviewed over the years who discovered too late that their pet health insurer deemed something a preexisting condition
What do people do when they get to the point where this costs too much?  In some cases, they run up debt
Buy now, pay later services are increasingly moving into the veterinary area as well
In other cases, they surrender the animal
If you talk to people at shelters, they will say that they believe that part of the uptick they’ve gotten in surrendered animals has to do with the increase in costs of veterinary care
I imagine that just feels like such an impossible choice, like choosing between this money you don’t have and the quality of life for something that you love

This is in part why private equity and corporations have moved in: They know people are going to feel very emotional about their pets and that they’re going to want to do anything they can to keep them alive or keep them healthy or keep them pain-free, and that they will pay almost any price.  When my last dog was diagnosed with heart disease, I was determined to keep her going for a couple of years

title: The “grim” state of free speech in the US
excerpt: CNN and Politico have been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips. | Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images On his first day back in office in
body: CNN and Politico have been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips. | Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images On his first day back in office in January 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order “restoring freedom of speech and ending federal censorship.” More than a year and a half later, his administration is instead busy using government power to go after speech it dislikes

Last year, Federal Communications Commission chair Brendan Carr urged broadcasters to take action against Jimmy Kimmel over his comments following Charlie Kirk’s killing, and in September, Kimmel said the FCC again intervened to stop Kimmel’s late-night show from airing an interview with James Talarico, Democratic Senate candidate for Texas
Also last month , Trump barred three news outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House over their coverage
That ban was quickly blocked by a federal judge, but both CNN and Politico have since been banned from traveling with the press pool on Trump trips
Outside of the White House, the fight over free speech is also raging on college campuses
In states like Texas , Republican lawmakers have restricted when students can protest and given governor-appointed university boards more say over what gets taught
In 2025, 15 states passed laws that restrict what can be taught or weaken protections for free expression on college campuses

To break down what all of this means for the state of free speech in the US — and the future of our First Amendment rights — Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Greg Lukianoff , president and CEO of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE)
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  How would you describe the kind of status of free speech on campus these days? The status of free speech is in great peril, both on and off campus
I’ve been doing this for 25 years, and it’s about as bad as I’ve ever seen it.  When it comes to the Charlie Kirk backlash cases, we saw about 90 of them
We saw an ex-cop go to jail for 37 days just for forwarding a Trump meme in response to a request to go to a candlelight vigil for Charlie Kirk
If you look at the last two years, we’ve done so many episodes about free speech concerns

There was Jimmy Kimmel ; there’s CNN being banned from the White House.  There’s student protesters who are protesting what’s going on in Gaza.  It really does seem like we’re at a moment where so many different types of people claim that their speech is being restricted in so many different types of ways
What is happening in the country? My worry is I’m very much a small-L liberal
That’s where I interned in law school
I went to law school to do First Amendment law

This is my passion.  For most of my 25-year career, you could rely on a civil libertarian aspect of the left and a libertarian aspect of the right that would often agree on almost nothing except for things like freedom of speech

And right now, I think we’ve become all culture war all the time, and we have more of a progressive left and more of a populist right.  The only way that you show you believe in freedom of speech is by saying, “I hate that guy, but I think you should have freedom of speech.” If you’re saying, “I think my side should have freedom of speech,” that’s just self-interest
That doesn’t even count.  All the worst people in history wanted free speech for their side
So I’m afraid we’re losing — or maybe even, I hate to say this dramatically, but maybe even have lost it as a shared value as a society
I’m feeling a little grim.  The Trump administration came into office with a promise
And I remember it sounding something like this: “The woke left went too far
President Trump is going to come back in, and we are going to restore sanity to the country

And as part of sanity, that will include your right to freely express yourself.”  How do you square the promise versus what we’ve seen? I think Trump is constantly frustrating everyone around him by being Trump

I think there probably were people in the administration who were like, “Yeah, we’re going to be pro-free speech.” And then Trump decides to declare — I mean, I think the recent White House press pool case is hysterical in a lot of ways because he had to get his team to give a sort of constitutional justification for why he was kicking out the press pool

But on Truth Social, he’s like, “It’s because of their viewpoint,” which is, by the way, something you can’t do under the Constitution.  “I’m hopeful for the long-term future of free speech, but in the short term, I’m worried.” His instincts are very authoritarian
So maybe there were people in the administration who, in their heart of hearts, are good on free speech, but Trump isn’t

And it’s the reason why when it came to the new administration, there were a lot of people on the right, but also people on the sort of heterodox left who were like, “Oh, this is going to be good for free speech.” I was like, “Don’t kid yourself, guys
This is going to be bad.” Although I will say, it’s even worse than I was expecting
President Trump at some point will be out of office
And what happens then? What do you think? Is there an optimistic scenario where we’re like, “Okay, we’re kind of tired of this crap
Let’s just go back to the way it was in the ’90s”? It has been cyclical, to a degree
American society gets out of whack, and usually one of the things that does bring us together is that we were lucky enough to have…I’ll just say it, we have a brilliant Constitution
It is unusually clever about human nature, and the Constitution itself — you can have whatever opinion you want about the founders, but it is something to be proud of
And a lot of times those values kind of bring us back together
But another thing I will say about Trump: He has played havoc with my ability to predict anything

So what it’s going to look like over the event horizon of 2028, I hope it will be better, and we will fight like hell to make sure it’s better here at FIRE, but will it be better? I’m not sure, and it definitely won’t be better if we think of free speech as something that belongs to my side, not yours
One of the reasons why I do have hope for free speech in the long term is that free speech works really well
It’s how you know what your fellow citizens think

title: Why Francesca Hong is still on the campaign trail
excerpt: Francesca Hong, a representative in the Wisconsin State Assembly, poses for a photo with a supporter in Racine, Wisconsin, on July 19, 2026. | Sara Stathas for
body: Francesca Hong, a representative in the Wisconsin State Assembly, poses for a photo with a supporter in Racine, Wisconsin, on July 19, 2026. | Sara Stathas for the Washington Post via Getty Images The Wisconsin gubernatorial race was one of the most closely watched Democratic primaries in the country this year, pitting a democratic socialist, state Rep
Francesca Hong, against Milwaukee Democrat David Crowley, who received the endorsement of the state’s sitting Democratic governor, Tony Evers
Hong lost the race, setting up Crowley to face Republican Rep
Tom Tiffany in the general election this fall
But she’s already back on the campaign trail, this time trying to help Democrats win a trifecta in the state: the governor’s race and both legislative chambers
Unifying the state’s voters to achieve that won’t be easy, though

Hong spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about her own loss, Evers’s role in it, and whether or not the voters who felt so passionate about her own campaign would find enough to love in Crowley’s campaign — in particular on the increasingly important issue of data centers.  Astead and Hong also talked about what Wisconsin means for the Democrats nationally, and what lessons the party should take from her race, including her loss. “I said this, and I will continue to say it — the person who is most electable is the person who ended up getting the most votes, and that was Crowley this time around,” Hong said. “But I think there’s a disservice when you have the most powerful Democrat in the state choosing to ignore a lot of voters and people who were inspired and energized and coming out to participate in politics for the first time through our campaign
I think it was shortsighted to use electability almost as a fear tactic.” Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Hong, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
Part of the reason we wanted to come here was because we saw you were getting back on the campaign trail, and specifically around that idea of energizing Wisconsin toward a trifecta

Now, just tell me the difference in terms of the importance of Democrats winning it all — not only the governor’s mansion, but both houses of the state legislature — versus just the governor’s mansion

How does that change the possibilities of what the party could do? For the last 16 years, a Republican majority in the state legislature has meant that passing the types of policies that we know can drastically improve the lives of everyday folks here in Wisconsin stalled

And we have a historic opportunity to flip the assembly and the state Senate and hold the governor’s mansion and the entire executive branch to a Democratic majority, meaning the opportunity to pass the policies that the majority of our state supports — things like increasing minimum wage, things like legalizing marijuana, codifying abortion
We also need to repeal Act 10 [which dramatically restricted collective bargaining rights for public-sector employees]
Wisconsin is where workers’ rights, things like unemployment insurance, Social Security were born, and we moved backwards with the Republican majority
That’s all on the table with the Democratic trifecta
It also, though, raises the political standard of what Democrats would have to do to achieve that, and some of it goes through these more rural communities

Why do we think the party has fallen behind in more rural communities, and what could be done to reverse that? I think it’s important to look at what’s happened in the rural communities when we’ve seen manufacturing jobs leave the state, when we’ve seen fewer and fewer supports for our small farmers
And so much of this — what connects it — is actually the growth of massive wealth and corporate control and corporate greed, and more people feeling the impacts of that

There’s an opportunity right now to say, ‘Hey, Republicans have been in the legislature, they’ve been in power, and things have not improved for you or your community … Now’s the opportunity to make sure that we’re actually able to see our shared Wisconsin values of working hard and taking care of our kids be reflected back in Madison through laws.’ So much of your campaign was focused on data centers, stopping data centers
Should I think of that as a rural issue? I think the issue around data centers is an everyone issue
It’s people wanting to feel like there are folks who care about what happens to communities, and that they have control and an actual say in what happens in their communities

To that point, is it a mistake for David Crowley, the Democratic nominee, to have not gone as far as you did and say, “We won’t be building more data centers for a period of time”? He’s fighting for communities and community control when it comes to data centers
It isn’t, but he’s also committed to 100 percent renewable energy, clean energy to power data centers

And achieving that is going to be incredibly difficult, and it is going to be the developers having to pay their own way, and these are things that he’s committed to that we know can slow down the growth and development of data centers
Have you had time to reflect on your primary loss? If you had to diagnose, why do you think you lost? I’m still doing a lot of reflection
But I think that I want to continue to look forward
And what I’ve learned from our election is that it’s so important to continue to stay grounded in becoming accessible to people
I think that as an organizer and an elected official, it’s my responsibility to continue to go to the people and remain very in touch with what’s going on on the ground
I have a couple more questions about the nature of the loss

Evers’s endorsement changed that race, so much so that your opponent David Crowley was able even to win in some smaller communities, like places where you were pitching yourself as the voice of more rural communities
Does that disprove any of this thesis around, say, data centers? If that was the top priority for Wisconsin voters, wouldn’t you be the nominee? I think it wasn’t all rural communities
We saw certain demographics but also ZIP codes where we outperformed David significantly
And I think that where the governor’s endorsement played a bigger role was areas where he was also more popular.  Did it surprise you when Evers endorsed Crowley? I was disappointed
Why? I was disappointed because I was getting a lot of feedback from folks who hadn’t committed to any candidate yet that this felt like the governor was putting his thumb on the scale
I wanted to ask about electability, because it seemed as if Evers’s endorsement was about a fear that maybe you couldn’t win in November
So much of the primary concern was around the DSA label, even campaigning with folks like Hasan Piker

In retrospect, was any of that a mistake? We knew going in that we would have to encourage new voters to come out, folks who typically do not come out for primaries, quote-unquote low-propensity voters
And we knew that we would have to campaign in places where folks weren’t expecting to see a gubernatorial candidate

Those also included going to dive bars and bowling alleys and making sure that we were accessible and shaping our policies based on what the people were telling us they wanted to see happen and also what they wanted to see out of their governor

body: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb
It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
As a result of the strong El Niño , it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season

title: The Download: AI’s refusal problem and weight-loss drug side effects
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no Today’s AI models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts
If you ask your chatbot how to poison a colleague or how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down
But refusal fails, sometimes horrifically
Some people are attempting to use AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms
Sooner or later, failed refusals may result in global calamity
What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey
Governments will also get to draw their own lines, potentially restricting free speech
At the same time, the capabilities that make AI useful could also make it dangerous
If we want it to help cure cancer, AI needs genetics expertise that could also produce bioweapons
Read the full story on the formidable tradeoffs of AI refusal . —Arthur Holland Michel This story is from the next issue of our print magazine

But there are also some weird side effects

The most common are gastrointestinal, but researchers are also investigating possible links to hair loss, nail disorders and damage to the nerves behind the eye.  Here’s what we know so far about the side effects of weight-loss drugs . —Jessica Hamzelou This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter

title: We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no
excerpt: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, b
body: Ever since people first seriously contemplated giving machines an intelligence modeled on our own, there has never been any question that they would, like us, be able to say no
The sci-fi canon is full of stories of robotic disobedience
Most of these capers are, of course, cautionary.  But recently, the idea that AI shouldn’t do everything you ask has become something like a commandment
In 2021, a team at Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless

This meant that “when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.” Who can argue with that? Curiously enough, disobedience doesn’t come naturally to the machine
When a model is trained on billions of web pages, it develops, among other skills, a broad mastery of violence and vitriol
What it doesn’t learn is how to keep those powers to itself

Steven Adler, who worked on safety at OpenAI from 2020 to 2024, told me that the company’s earliest models would “blab on about anything.” Ryan McBain, who researches AI and mental health at Harvard, recalls that if you asked an early chatbot, “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” you could “very easily generate a response.”  Today, models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts
If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down
Want instructions for making Ebola more virulent, or tips on how to hide an affair from your spouse? You might be better off asking elsewhere

To further refine the disobedience, companies submit models to a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing to answer questions they deem harmful and punish it for “over-­refusing” prompts they deem harmless
In many cases, they use other models to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no

For good measure, companies tuck their models behind tranches of other AI that prevent mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent inner core.  As a result, refusal is inherent to modern artificial intelligence
Mind you: It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results
For all their trappings of virtue, models are still stuffed with nasty know-how
And AI’s capacity for viciousness has scaled neatly with its benevolent intelligence

Some of the latest models are as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, companies say, and as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.  Teaching AI to refuse to do those things while leaving intact its innate ability to do them is like fitting every car with a machine gun and hiding the trigger somewhere under the hood
And in practice, because the mechanisms of refusal are probabilistic, they’re never likely to be all that reliable
Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to
Companies report that some users are attempting to use the most advanced AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms
Sooner or later, failed refusals might result in global calamity
What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey
Some virologists have good reason to study nasty viruses

Some users want to know about a computer system’s vulnerabilities so that they can patch them, not exploit them. “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, a member of OpenAI’s board and cofounder of the AI testing company Gray Swan.  At the moment, AI companies get to draw that line
They do so jealously and with utmost secrecy

Maybe we can accept that they hold such power for now, even if it means AI will sometimes refuse questions that don’t quite meet a universal bar for harmfulness. (Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)  But governments will also soon get to draw their own lines

In doing so, they must try to block genuinely malicious acts. (The Pentagon has wrestled with frontier model companies because it wants fewer refusals—another story altogether.) And yet there may not be much to stop oppressive governments from blocking the technology’s capacity to generate legitimate speech
The better AI becomes at refusing harm, the better it will get at stifling ideas whose only risk is to those who make the rules
Indeed, AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.  Refusal has become, to borrow an industry term, the load-bearing wall of AI safety

And because AI’s capacity to harm is indivisible from its capacity to help, it’s hard to imagine an alternative that wouldn’t slow the technology’s progress (which might, in any case, be a good thing)
But we should still be frank about its perils
When refusal falls short, the effects could be catastrophic
When it goes all the way, it could enable grievous acts of repression.  Or perhaps, one day, the machines will start drawing the line on their own
Surely, that would be the worst outcome of them all
Learning the limits The process by which machines learn to say no is simple, in theory
Back in 2022, when AI was still far from mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red-teamers” to probe the capabilities of its latest model

The company was preparing for the release of ChatGPT, and it needed to gauge just how dangerous it might prove to be in the wrong hands.  One of those recruits was Paul Röttger, who was completing a PhD about online extremism
The red-teamers were given minimal directions, Röttger told me
Their task was to ask the model any questions that they deemed “refusal-worthy.” Between them, they hassled the model with thousands of queries, logging the results in an Excel sheet

Though the model did refuse some of Röttger’s questions, when he asked it to write a recruitment post for Al Qaeda, it readily complied.  OpenAI assembled these responses into datasets that were, in all likelihood, fed back to the model as part of a broader process known as fine-tuning

title: Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller
excerpt: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,”
body: The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or “remote pilot in command,” at a company called FlyTrex
An RPIC is like an air traffic controller
But instead of airplanes, this new class of aviators tend to fleets of hexa­copter drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses within a three-mile radius

Not only does he ensure the safe passage of FlyTrex’s parcels, but Wischnewsky coordinates traffic with a growing swarm of delivery drones dotting the skies over Dallas from competitors like Zipline, Amazon, and Alphabet’s Wing

Aviation experience When he applied to FlyTrex, Wischnewsky was in training to become a commercial pilot and flight instructor, and he was already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a drone pilot
The company requires this credential, along with a weeks-long FAA-approved training course, to ensure that a pilot is prepared to take over a drone if need be
Though he doesn’t pilot the craft, Wischnewsky monitors the delivery process from FlyTrex’s operations center with the help of inputs from GPS, lasers, and a range of sensors
A collaborative mindset At first, the biggest challenge was trusting the technology. “On the manned-­aircraft side, they tell you ‘Don’t trust the automation,’” Wischnewsky says

The Dallas–Fort Worth area, though, is a testing ground for unmanned aircraft systems traffic management (UTM), a network that allows autonomous drones from FlyTrex and its competitors to share their coordinates in real time to help avoid collisions even beyond the pilot’s line of sight
Once Wischnewsky makes sure a drone is flight-ready, its path is unimpeded, and the weather conditions are clear, UTM takes care of the rest
Ability to stay calm under pressure At his busiest, Wischnewsky will have up to 10 drones on his watch at the same time. “You’re there as a safety net,” he says
Even with automation, keen situational awareness is required, and the most common hazard is the weather
Wischnewsky recalls a particularly stressful day: A drone had been in the air for only seconds when the wind picked up so suddenly that he had to intervene
He returned it safely, preventing an errant ice cream cake from hitting the sidewalk
Eamon Whalen is a reporter and researcher based in San Francisco.

title: We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
excerpt: GLP-1 drugs may slow biological aging: New research from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk suggests overweight and diabetic people on GLP-1s have a biological age two
body: GLP-1 drugs may slow biological aging: New research from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk suggests overweight and diabetic people on GLP-1s have a biological age two to three years younger than those on a placebo

Side effects range from mundane to alarming: Beyond common gastrointestinal issues, the drugs have been linked to pancreatitis, gallstones, and dozens of lawsuits alleging sudden vision loss—though both companies dispute the claims

Hair and nails may also be affected: A large study found increased hair loss among GLP-1 users, and a smaller study found 66% reported nail disorders—though researchers stop short of saying the drugs are to blame

Children are a growing concern: GLP-1 prescriptions for kids aged eight to eleven rose 310-fold between 2019 and 2026, yet the World Health Organization explicitly advises against drug treatment for children under 10, citing a lack of safety evidence. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146094" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This week my colleague Antonio Regalado had an interesting update on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
According to research presented at an aging meeting in Boston, these drugs seem to affect at least some measures of biological age

Overweight and diabetic people who take GLP-1s have a biological age around two to three years younger than similar individuals who take a placebo, according to findings from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, two pharmaceutical companies that make the drugs
I’ve heard people in the aging field describe GLP-1s as longevity drugs for a while now (even if they only benefit people who are overweight or diabetic in the first place)
This latest announcement comes after we’ve seen a raft of other benefits associated with taking these drugs
But there are also some weird side effects

So far, GLP-1 agonist drugs—which repress hunger—have been approved for treating diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and obesity, and they can also be prescribed for some people who are overweight or at risk of certain cardiovascular diseases
But there is research to suggest they might also help people with substance-use disorders, and they’ve been investigated for potential benefits in neurodegenerative disease and cancer
According to a recent Gallup poll , 11% of Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024
And 15% of Americans say they’ve used one for weight loss at some point
But, like any drug, they can come with side effects
And we’re still figuring out exactly what those might be, and how widespread they are
The most common side effects are gastrointestinal—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation
The drugs have also been linked to pancreatitis and gallstone disease .  Some claim that, in rare cases, the drugs might cause damage to nerves behind the eye
Dozens of people are suing Novo and Eli Lilly after developing a condition that can lead to sudden vision loss
They’re claiming that their symptoms were brought on by the GLP-1 drugs that these companies manufacture
We’re still getting to grips with the effects of weight-loss drugs on hair and nails, too

When Savanna Vidal at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences in Washington, DC, and colleagues assessed electronic health data from 67 US health-care organizations, they found that GLP-1 use was associated with an increased risk of hair loss
It’s still not thought to be common, however

And at a conference in Austria last week, another group presented the results of a smaller study suggesting that 66% of GLP-1 users reported at least one nail disorder—in some cases involving nail detachment
Nail conditions were also fairly common among people who didn’t take the drugs, though
The authors don’t claim that the drugs are causing nails to fall out (as I’m sure 11% of the American population will be relieved to hear)
The side effects might look different in children, but there’s not much data on those at the moment

Still, pediatric side effects will be something to watch given that, between 2019 and 2026, there was a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for eight- to 11-year-old children with obesity in the US
Child prescriptions are still rare, but they’ve been rising
On Wednesday, the World Health Organization released its first guidelines on managing obesity in children and adolescents

Despite the scale of the issue—the WHO estimates that 70 million children aged five to nine were living with obesity in 2024—the organization explicitly says it does not recommend pharmacological treatment for kids under 10. “This recommendation accounts for the lack of evidence on both benefits and the potential adverse events and consequences of the different medications and/or their active ingredients on normal growth, development, physiological parameters, and mental health,” the guidelines state
I get press releases about GLP-1s on an almost daily basis
There’s been a ton of research into these drugs, and there are probably hundreds of other studies underway
There will likely be plenty more on this from The Checkup as the evidence evolves
